Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the simultaneously severe, poorly processed trauma-memory profile implied by 'Full Sensory Reliving' and 'Olfactory Recall'. Those latter items suggest intrusive sensory re-experiencing, while very easy verbal access points in the opposite direction and is hard to reconcile in the same profile without additional context.

The Threat node is not coherent internally: 'Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating' is a non-threat/cognitive impairment item, whereas the other threat items are specific hypervigilant danger-monitoring states ('Waking Alert', 'Startle to Movement'). This makes the Threat selections thematically inconsistent.

Cross-node coherence is weak around 'Triggers: Being Followed'. That trigger implies a persecutory/social-tracking danger theme, but the rest of the profile centers more on restraint, safety checking, startle, and sensory reliving, without corresponding appraisals or memories about pursuit/tracking. It feels insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation.

'Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out' is not well linked to the selected trigger/threat pattern. The profile emphasizes tiredness, restraint sensations, night-time safety checking, and movement-related startle, but not a clear outside/public-space threat theme. Avoiding going out therefore appears mismatched to the rest of the selected content.

vignette: Elena, a nineteen-year-old European-American dancer, had always found refuge in the rhythmic certainty of her routines. That sense of order was shattered one Tuesday evening during a rehearsal at the downtown loft theater when a sudden, low-frequency rumble rippled through the building. An unseen fire, ignited by a faulty electrical line, spread rapidly, filling the air with acrid smoke and the metallic scent of burning stage carpet. Emergency crews swarmed the backstage area, but the narrow stairwell was blocked by debris. In the chaos, Elena was caught beneath a falling proscenium arch; a stagehand's hand, desperate to pull her out, restrained her shoulders so firmly she could feel the metal hook digging into her skin. The collapse left her gasping, her heart pounding, and her limbs trembling with exhaustion. She never saw a clear image of the moment she was physically held back; instead, a jarring, muffled memory flooded her-sudden darkness, the weight of a hand, the distant wail of alarms. The injustice of the accident, coupled with the sense that no one could be held accountable for the negligence that led to it, seeded a belief in her that the world was unfair and that she belonged nowhere. The first time Elena's sense of fatigue, the scent of smoke, and the lingering feeling of a hand gripping her arms brought back that night's memory, she reacted by refusing to leave the studio. The exhaustion she felt made her want to stay within the familiar walls; the knowledge that the crowd outside might be "following" her in some uncanny way-whether through the echo of her own heartbeats or the subtle gaze of strangers-made her hide her face with her hands whenever she entered the hallway. Her belief that nothing had been done to rectify the disaster-her sense of injustice-only amplified this avoidance, as did her conviction that if she thought about the event she would be overwhelmed. When the full sensory reliving of the collapse surged, Elena could not find words to describe the terror, so she stopped enjoying the very dance that had once defined her. The startle she felt at any sudden movement-whether a prop shifting or a partner's brush-was a threat that pushed her into a state of hyper-vigilance. That hyper-alertness, in turn, made her concentration fail, forcing her to withdraw from rehearsals. The sleepless nights spent waking to check if she was safe reinforced the threat of being followed. All of these elements fed back: her avoidance of going out increased her fatigue, which triggered further memories; her face-hiding made it harder to focus, exacerbating the threat of distraction; the memory's vividness strengthened her negative appraisal of injustice, which pushed her deeper into avoidance. In short, the triggers of tiredness, being followed, and the tactile sensation of restraint both sprang from and fed into the memory and the threat, while each of those components drove Elena toward maladaptive strategies that, by turning her attention back to the triggers and the threat, closed the loop that trapped her in the aftermath of the disaster. In the months that followed, the cycle became a living part of Elena's routine. She would arrive at the studio only to stay within the first rehearsal room, turning her face into the wall so no one could see her. Whenever the lights flickered or a stagehand moved abruptly, she would jump, the sudden motion reminding her of the arch's collapse. The exhaustion from her self-imposed isolation left her muscles sore and her mind foggy, making it impossible to rehearse choreography that demanded focus. Her teacher, noticing her declining performance, suggested she take a break, but Elena's fear of the world's unfairness made even that idea unbearable. Friends began to withdraw, sensing her growing discomfort, and the sense that she belonged nowhere hardened into a quiet resignation that her life had become a series of narrow, safe spaces. Today, Elena finally seeks help after a particularly harsh night when a distant siren startled her awake, and she spent an hour pacing in her small apartment, trying to convince herself she was safe. The most profound fear she carries now is that the next startle will collapse her world again, and the deepest hope she clings to is to relearn the rhythm of her own body without the constant echo of that night's terror.
